comments.author: @lilywhitesoh9545
comments.text:
Vietnam’s economy relies heavily on foreign companies attracted by cheap labor. This creates jobs, but it doesn’t mean Vietnamese companies are developing their own core technologies. As wages rise, foreign companies can simply move to cheaper countries. Without globally competitive domestic companies and advanced technologies of its own, Vietnam risks remaining a low-cost assembly hub rather than becoming a developed country.

Vietnam faces an even bigger challenge in acquiring core technologies and developing its own industries. It cannot compete with China’s price competitiveness or South Korea and Japan’s technological expertise and product quality. If Vietnam cannot compete on price, quality, or advanced technology, how can it move up the global value chain? Cheap labor alone will never be enough to become a developed country.

replies.author: @lilywhitesoh9545
replies.text:
@t@ttran2212 Companies choose Vietnam for low labor costs, trade agreements, tax incentives, and supply-chain diversification, not necessarily because Vietnam has superior manufacturing capabilities. Being chosen as a production base doesn’t mean owning the technology behind the products.

Look at VinFast. It has accumulated enormous losses for years while relying on international suppliers for critical components, including batteries, semiconductors, and electronic systems. Its partnership with China’s Gotion for LFP battery technology is one example. The battery is one of the most important and expensive parts of an EV, and assembling cars with foreign-sourced technology is not the same as independently mastering the entire supply chain.

VinFast’s sales in India don’t prove technological superiority either. Aggressive pricing and market expansion can increase sales without demonstrating sustainable profitability or superior manufacturing efficiency.

Attracting factories and selling cars is one thing; developing advanced technology and producing competitively at a profit is another. Don’t confuse the two.

Honestly, cut the delusion. Vietnam’s manufacturing “boom” is literally just riding on China’s back.

Companies aren't choosing Vietnam because it's technologically superior; they choose it for total cost, tax perks, and most importantly, its proximity to China's massive supply chain. You guys don't invent or build anything advanced from scratch—you just import machinery, battery cells, and electronic components from China and other countries, then screw them together. 

Even look at VinFast. Selling cars at aggressive prices while losing billions of dollars every single year isn't "superior efficiency." They rely on foreign suppliers like CATL, Gotion, and Samsung SDI for critical EV tech. Assembling imported parts in a local factory doesn't mean you mastered the technology or the supply chain.

Vietnam isn't beating China; it's surviving purely because China is right next door, making it a convenient hub to bypass US tariffs. Don't confuse being a cheap assembly garage with having actual technological superiority. Stop exposing your ignorance like this—you clearly have no idea what you're talking about.

comments.author: @pineapplesareyummy6352
comments.text: Vietnam is well governed under the CPV. Their system is very similar to ours, so naturally, I'd expect Vietnam to get similar results. As for comparison with Japan, it wouldn't surprise me to see Vietnam overtake Japan, because Japan's population is falling. Vietnam will have more people than Japan at some point, so it comes down to per capita. China's GDP per capital (nominal or PPP) is already 40-50% of Japan's level - something I would not have expected in the 1990s, whereas today, I will no longer be surprised if China passes Japan before 2050. Korea has already done it. But I don't agree with your opening statement that the other countries in Southeast Asia "failed". Malaysia is a rich country with a hi-tech economy, and maintains high economic growth for its current level. Thailand is also solidly upper-middle income. The problems with some of the others like Philippines is just because corruption/kleptocracy is uniquely bad there. Under Duterte, Philippines could have become more like Vietnam, as he was cleaning up both drugs and corruption and adopted a good foreign policy of non-alignment (or multilateral alignment). Now, they have a leader who is literally the son of Ferdinand and Imelda. The apple doesn't fall far from the tree....
